n: Ezra picks up exactly where 2 Chronicles ends. In Cyrus’s first year ruling Babylon (538 BC), God moved the Persian king’s heart to fulfill Jeremiah’s prophecy of a return after seventy years. God can work through foreign rulers to keep His promises.

f.w: the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah

n: Cyrus’s decree credits Israel’s God with giving him his empire and charging him to build a temple in Jerusalem. Persian kings often honored local gods to win loyalty, but scripture sees God’s hand at work.

f.g: A title often used for Israel’s God in the Persian period.

n: Anyone among God’s people may go up to Jerusalem to rebuild the house of the God of Israel. “Go up” is the language of pilgrimage and return.

f.g: Cyrus’s decree acknowledges Him as the God who dwells in Jerusalem.

n: Those who stayed behind were to support the returnees with silver, gold, goods, and animals, plus freewill offerings for the temple. This recalls Israel leaving Egypt with gifts from their neighbors — a second exodus.

f.w: help him with silver, and with gold

n: The family heads of Judah and Benjamin, with priests and Levites — everyone whose spirit God stirred — prepared to go. Not all exiles returned; many had settled comfortably in Babylon. Those who went had been moved by God.

f.w: them whose spirit God had raised

n: Their neighbors supported them with silver, gold, goods, livestock, and valuables, besides freewill offerings.
Cyrus returned the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had carried off and placed in his gods’ temple. The sacred vessels coming home signaled true restoration.

f.w: the vessels of the house of the LORD

n: Cyrus had Mithredath the treasurer count them out to Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah. Sheshbazzar may be the official title-holder or another name linked to Zerubbabel; scholars debate this.

f.g: A Persian name meaning ‘given by Mithra.’
The first governor of the returnees; whether he is the same as Zerubbabel is debated.

n: The inventory begins: thirty gold dishes, a thousand silver dishes, and twenty-nine knives (or pans). Careful counting showed respect for holy things.
Thirty gold bowls, 410 lesser silver bowls, and a thousand other vessels.
There were 5,400 gold and silver items in all, which Sheshbazzar brought from Babylon to Jerusalem with the exiles. (The listed items add to 2,499, so the total may include unlisted pieces.)

f.g: The itemized numbers sum to fewer; the total probably includes items not itemized.
